data.content_ref: inline:The argument fails because Popper's own concept of verisimilitude was rigorously shown to be logically untenable within his framework. In 1974, David Miller and Tichý independently proved that, given Popper's definitions, a false theory can never be said to have greater verisimilitude than another false theory based on test results alone; the comparison collapses unless one assumes inductive probability (that passing tests makes truth more likely). By relying on verisimilitude as the mechanism to justify preferring corroborated theories, the target invokes a concept that Popper himself had to abandon or significantly revise because it secretly presupposes the very inductive logic he sought to reject. Therefore, the preference is not defensible on 'Popper's own terms' as stated, but rather requires an inductive bridge the target explicitly denies.
